episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, March 16, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education. At Metropolitan State University Denver, faculty are facing challenges in validating online assessments in the age of A.I. <break time="0.5s"/>

In Insights & Trends today, according to Denver7, Metropolitan State University Denver is grappling with the complexities of student assessment in the A.I. era. Jeff Loats, professor and director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU, expressed concerns about the validity of online assessments, stating, "we don't know how to do that in a valid way." Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, views this as an opportunity to improve assessment practices. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer has modified his journalism class to feature online lectures and in-person assignments, a strategy aimed at reducing A.I.'s ability to complete tasks unauthentically. Schafer also noted the difficulty for instructors to adapt their teaching methods, as faculty buy-in varies. Some professors permit limited A.I. use, while others restrict it entirely, resulting in a patchwork approach. The challenge of establishing definitive guidelines across more than 100 majors at MSU highlights the evolving nature of institutional responses. <break time="0.75s"/>

Turning to Case Study today, Universidad Austral, in collaboration with Universidad de La Sabana, has developed an intelligent dashboard for student assessment, as reported by Times Higher Education. This tool allows students and educators to engage with A.I. as both a teammate and a teaching assistant. It offers continuous feedback and aids students in honing their judgment regarding A.I. usage. <break time="0.75s"/>

Meanwhile, in Practical Tips, the San Diego Community College District is set to host "InnovAItion Day" on March 20, according to City Times. The event will unite faculty, staff, and students to discuss responsible A.I. use in education. It will feature student-led panels and discussions about the role of A.I. in learning environments. <break time="0.75s"/>

Over at UNC Greensboro, in another Case Study, the School of Nursing has appointed A.I. Champions to integrate artificial intelligence throughout its curriculum, simulation, and faculty training, as noted by UNC Greensboro. With 70 percent of faculty actively using A.I. tools, the initiative aims to enhance student engagement and accommodate diverse learning styles. <break time="0.75s"/>

And here's one worth watching from the Case Study file. George Washington University Professor Michael Tadesse has restructured his marketing courses to foster an "innovation mindset lab," as reported by GW Today. In this setting, students collaborate with real businesses to develop A.I.-enabled prototypes. This approach prioritizes strategic thinking and adaptability over traditional content delivery. <break time="0.75s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

topStory.headline: MSU Denver Faculty Say Online Assessments Have Become Impossible to Validate
topStory.summary:
At Metropolitan State University Denver, faculty are confronting challenges with student assessment in the A.I. age, according to Denver7. Jeff Loats, professor and director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU, stated that if assessments are online, "we don't know how to do that in a valid way."

Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, described this as an opportunity to "right the ship" on assessment practices. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer described flipping his journalism class from in-person lectures with online assignments to online lectures with in-person assignments. He anticipates more case studies and "apply this to your life, apply to your community" assignments because these are harder for A.I. to complete authentically.

Schafer acknowledged that it is difficult for instructors to drastically change their teaching methods, and faculty buy-in varies. Some professors allow limited A.I. use while others restrict it entirely, creating a patchwork approach. The challenge of creating definitive guidelines across more than 100 majors at MSU illustrates how institutional responses are still evolving.

stories.headline: No-Code A.I. Tools Expand Access for Academic Users
stories.summary: New analysis highlights how no-code A.I. platforms enable students and faculty to leverage artificial intelligence without programming expertise, according to Open Source For You. Tools range from Google Teachable Machine for beginners to research assistants for literature review.
